title: Building your project by talking to the AI
intro: You're going to build something real of your own — a website, a store, a tool for your work — without writing a single line of code. You tell it in plain English what you want, the AI hands you the files, you save them and open them on your computer, and you keep asking for changes until it looks like what you had in mind. By the end you'll have a page working in front of you and you'll know how to keep improving it on your own.

theory.title: The AI does what you tell it, no more and no less
theory.text: It doesn't read your mind. It builds what you describe, and it makes up the rest however it likes. If you say "build me a website", you'll get one of its generic websites, with filler text that says nothing. If you say "a page for my ceramics studio in the arts district, with class schedules, photos of the pieces, and a button to message me on WhatsApp", you'll get that. The difference between a result you can use and one you throw away is almost never about how smart the AI is: it's about how many details you gave it.
theory.analogy: It's like ordering a bookshelf from a carpenter over the phone. If all you say is "a bookshelf", you get whatever he had in mind. If you say the space it needs to fill, the height, the wood, and what it's for, you get yours.

theory.title: What it hands you back is text files, nothing more
theory.text: A webpage is a text file whose name ends in .html. Nothing magical: you open it with Notepad and you see letters. What makes it look like a nice page is that the browser knows how to read those letters and paint them on screen. So the whole process boils down to the same thing over and over: the AI writes the text, you paste it into a file, give it the right name, and open it with the browser. If you name it wrong, the browser doesn't know what to do with it and shows you the raw text instead.
theory.analogy: Sheet music is paper with black marks until someone who knows how to play reads it. The browser is the one who knows how to play.

theory.title: The work loop: ask, save, look, correct
theory.text: Nobody gets it right on the first try, neither you nor the AI. The real work is circling back to the same spot: you ask for something, you save the file, you open it, you see what's wrong, and you tell it. Each lap takes you a couple of minutes and fixes one thing. Projects that turn out well aren't the ones asked for best the first time — they're the ones that went through twenty laps instead of three.
theory.analogy: Like trying on clothes: you don't stick with the first size you grab, you step out of the fitting room, look in the mirror, and go back in.

theory.title: One change at a time, and the whole file
theory.text: If you ask for five things at once, it'll get three right, one so-so, and it'll make up the last one, and you won't know which broke what. Ask for one thing at a time and check before moving on. And always ask for the complete file, first line to last, not just the piece it touched. When it gives you loose fragments, you have to figure out yourself where they fit, and that's exactly the point where people get stuck and give up on the project.
theory.analogy: It's the difference between the tailor handing you back the whole jacket repaired, versus handing you a loose sleeve and a "you sew it on yourself".

theory.title: Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini: all three work, the details vary
theory.text: All three can do this, and all three have a free version you can start with today without paying anything. Claude tends to write cleaner code and shows you the page working in a side window as it builds it, which is genuinely nice for this. ChatGPT is the best known and is more than capable for regular pages and tools. Gemini is the most generous with its free tier and is tightly connected to everything Google. The paid versions run around $20 a month each, and what you're mainly buying is being able to ask for a lot more per day. Pick one and stick with it: switching AIs mid-project means losing the thread of everything discussed.

theory.title: When chat gets too small for you: Claude Code
theory.text: Copy and paste works great until your project hits eight files. Past that, it gets tiring. Claude Code is the same AI, but installed on your computer and with permission to create and edit the files itself: you talk to it the same way, in plain English, and you never have to paste anything again. The price you pay is that it's operated from the terminal, that intimidating black window with text. Nobody's forcing you to make that leap today; the moment arrives on its own, when copy-paste starts bothering you more than the black window does. It's included in Claude's paid plan, around $20 a month.
theory.analogy: It's like going from dictating your grocery list to someone, to handing them the keys to your house so they also put the groceries away for you.

tasks.title: Pick an AI and open a new conversation
tasks.action: Go to claude.ai, chatgpt.com, or gemini.google.com and create a free account with your email, or log in if you already have one. The free version is more than enough for this guide, don't pay for anything yet. Open a new conversation with the button in the top left: on Claude and ChatGPT it says "New chat", on Gemini "New chat" as well. This conversation is going to be your whole project, so don't close it or switch to another one halfway through.
tasks.expect: An empty text box waiting for you to type, with no previous conversation above it.
tasks.stuck: If it asks for a phone number to verify the account, that's normal and only happens once. If it warns you that you've hit the usage limit, wait a few hours: the counter resets on its own.

tasks.title: Create the folder where your project will live
tasks.action: Go to your Desktop, right-click on an empty spot, and choose "New" → "Folder" (on Mac, "New Folder"). Name it my-project, in lowercase with a hyphen where a space would go. Everything the AI gives you gets saved in here and nowhere else, so you don't end up with loose files scattered in Downloads. No spaces or accented characters in the name: browsers get confused by them.
tasks.expect: A folder called my-project on your desktop, empty for now.

tasks.title: Tell it your idea and let it ask you questions
tasks.action: Copy the prompt below, replace the bracketed part with your actual idea, and paste it into the text box. You're not asking for code yet. Answer its questions in normal sentences, the way you'd tell a friend; if you don't know the answer to one, say "you decide" and move on.
tasks.prompt: I want to build [describe your idea in two or three sentences: what it is, who it's for, and what it needs to do]. I don't know how to code and I'm going to work by copying and pasting what you give me. Before writing any code, ask me five to eight questions, one at a time, to understand what I actually need. When it's clear, tell me, and give me a summary of what we're going to build.
tasks.expect: The AI asks you questions instead of handing you code, and at the end gives you a summary of your project that sounds like you.
tasks.stuck: If it hands you code straight away without asking anything, reply: "Stop. I don't want code yet. Ask me the questions first, one at a time".

tasks.title: Ask for the first file, complete and in one piece
tasks.action: Once the summary fits what you want, ask for the first version with the prompt below. You're asking for a single self-contained file that doesn't depend on anything you'd need to download separately. Wait for it to finish writing entirely before touching anything: it can take a good minute.
tasks.prompt: Great, go ahead. Build me a first version in a single file called index.html, with everything inside: the text, the styles, and whatever it needs to work. Don't use anything that has to be downloaded separately or links to external libraries; it needs to look good just by double-clicking to open the file. Give me the complete file, first line to last, not shortened anywhere and without writing "rest goes here". Use realistic sample text in English, no "Lorem ipsum".
tasks.expect: A large code block starting with <!DOCTYPE html> and ending with </html>, with a copy button above it. In Claude, also a live preview of the page on the right.
tasks.stuck: If it cuts off mid-sentence and stops, tell it "Continue exactly from where you left off" or "Give me the entire file again, without cutting it short".

tasks.title: Save the code into an .html file
tasks.action: Click the "Copy" button above the code block. Open Notepad (Windows: type "Notepad" in the Start menu) or TextEdit (Mac). Paste with Ctrl+V, or Cmd+V on Mac. Go to "File" → "Save As", go into your my-project folder, type the name index.html, and — this is what trips people up every time — in the "Save as type" dropdown choose "All Files" instead of "Text Documents". On Mac, before pasting anything, go to "Format" → "Make Plain Text", or TextEdit will save you a rich-text document instead of a webpage.
tasks.expect: Inside my-project, a file called index.html with your browser's icon (Chrome, Edge, Safari), not a notepad icon.
tasks.stuck: If the icon is a notepad icon, it got saved as index.html.txt. Rename it and remove the .txt at the end. If you can't see that part of the name, in File Explorer go to "View" → "Show" → "File name extensions".

tasks.title: Open it and see your project for the first time
tasks.action: Double-click index.html and it'll open in your browser. If it opens with another program, right-click → "Open with" → Chrome, or whatever browser you use. Look at the address bar: it shows something like file:///C:/Users/... That means you're viewing a file of your own, on your computer, with no internet involved. Nobody else can see it yet.
tasks.expect: Your page open in a browser tab, with your text, and looking like a real website.
tasks.stuck: If instead of a page you see a jumble of letters and symbols in raw text, the file got saved as plain text: go back to the previous task and repeat "Save As", choosing "All Files".

tasks.title: Ask for one change, just one
tasks.where: In the AI app, same conversation
tasks.action: Go back to the conversation and tell it what you want different, one thing only. Use the prompt below as a template. Then repeat the save process: copy, paste into Notepad, save over the same index.html, and refresh the browser tab with F5 (Cmd+R on Mac).
tasks.prompt: Change only this: [say what you want, with detail: "the contact button should be green and bigger", "remove the pricing section", "put the photos in three columns"]. Leave everything else exactly as it is. Give me the complete index.html file again, first line to last.
tasks.expect: When you refresh the browser, the change you asked for is there and the rest of the page is unchanged.
tasks.stuck: If fixing one thing broke another, just say so: "That change broke the top menu. Fix it and leave everything else exactly as it was".

tasks.title: Show it what you're seeing with a screenshot
tasks.where: On your computer and in the AI app
tasks.action: When something looks off and you don't know how to describe it in words, take a screenshot: on Windows press Windows + Shift + S and drag over the area, on Mac Cmd + Shift + 4. Then paste the image into the AI's text box with Ctrl+V and tell it what's bugging you. All three understand images and with a screenshot they get things right far more often than with a description.
tasks.expect: The image shows up as a thumbnail in the text box before you send it, and the AI replies describing what it sees in your screenshot.
tasks.stuck: If it won't let you paste it, look for the paperclip or plus icon next to the text box and upload it from there; screenshots usually end up in the Pictures folder or on the desktop.

tasks.title: Save a backup copy before a big change
tasks.action: Before asking for a major overhaul, right-click index.html → "Copy" and right-click an empty spot → "Paste". You'll get a file called index - copy.html; rename it to version-1.html. If the overhaul goes wrong, delete the broken index.html, duplicate version-1.html, and rename it index.html again. Warning: saving over a file overwrites it and there's no undo. Whatever was there before is gone, and the AI can't give it back to you, because it never had it in the first place.
tasks.expect: Two files in the folder: index.html and version-1.html. Double-clicking the second one shows you the earlier good version, intact.

tasks.title: Write the project brief so you don't start from scratch tomorrow
tasks.action: Conversations end: they hit their limit, get stuck, or you just leave and come back three days later. Ask it to summarize the project's status with the prompt below, copy what it gives you, and save it in a file called project.txt inside your folder, using Notepad, no worrying about file type this time. When you open a new conversation, the first thing you paste is that text.
tasks.prompt: Write me a summary for resuming this project in another conversation starting from scratch. Include: what we're building and for whom, what decisions we've already made, what files exist right now and what each one contains, what's left to do, and what broke along the way and how we fixed it. Write it assuming another AI that knows nothing will read it, so it can continue without asking me anything.
tasks.expect: A half-screen worth of text that, when you read it, tells your project's story better than you'd tell it to someone over the phone.

tasks.title: Try resuming the project in a new conversation
tasks.action: Open a new chat, paste the contents of project.txt, and add below it: "This is the state of my project. Ask me for the index.html file if you need it and let's continue". It's a cheap dry run: if the new AI understands where you left off, your brief works. If it loses the thread, go back to the old conversation and ask it to rewrite it with more detail.
tasks.expect: The new AI summarizes where things stood and proposes the next step without you having to explain anything else.
tasks.stuck: If it asks basic things that were already decided, your brief fell short: ask the AI in the old conversation to expand it, including the specific text and design decisions.

tasks.title: Decide whether it's worth jumping to Claude Code
tasks.where: On your computer, and only if you've outgrown chat
tasks.action: Do this only once your project passes four or five files and copy-paste starts feeling like a chore. Claude Code is installed from the terminal (Windows: search "PowerShell" in the Start menu; Mac: search "Terminal"). It's two commands you type and run by pressing Enter. The first, npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code, means "download the claude-code program and make it available system-wide": npm is the store these programs get downloaded from, and -g means "for the whole system". It needs Node installed first, which you download from nodejs.org by clicking the big button. The second, cd Desktop/my-project, means "go into my project's folder" (cd is "change directory"), and then you type claude, which starts the AI right there. From that point on you talk to it in plain English just like in chat, but it saves the files itself. It costs about $20 a month with the Claude Pro plan.
tasks.expect: A blinking cursor waiting for you to type, in plain English, with your my-project folder's path shown on screen. When you ask for the first change, you'll see it asks for permission before touching each file.
tasks.stuck: If a command responds "not recognized" or "command not found", Node is missing: install it from nodejs.org, close the black window, reopen it, and try again. And if all of this feels like too much, just leave it be: whole projects get finished with plain copy and paste.

canDo: Build a real website of your own, with your text and your photos, without writing code.
Change anything about it as many times as you need, just by describing it in your own words.
Make small tools that work on their own: a pricing calculator, a form, a timer, a price table.
See it all working on your computer before showing it to anyone.
Resume the project days later without having lost what was already discussed.
Get help with a screenshot when something looks wrong and you don't even know what it's called.
cantDo: Have someone else reach your page by typing an address: for now it only lives on your computer. Publishing it is the next step.
Actually charge money: that needs a payment gateway, and that data can't just sit loose in a file.
Store information that's still there tomorrow — users, orders, bookings: that needs a database.
Send emails or WhatsApp messages on its own from the file, even if the button looks like it does.
Trust everything it tells you: it makes up facts, prices, and addresses with striking confidence. Check anything that matters.
Carry a big project through in a single conversation without ever saving the project brief.
words: What you write to the AI. A request in plain, everyday English; the more specific, the better it turns out.
The specific brain answering you. Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini each have several, and the best ones are usually behind the paid plan.
The text with instructions that the computer understands. You don't write it: you copy it, paste it, and save it.
The letters at the end of a file's name (.html, .txt, .jpg). They tell the computer which program to open it with. Get it wrong and nothing works.
The language webpages are written in. An .html file is a page.
What the AI can hold in mind within a conversation. When it fills up, it starts forgetting the beginning; that's why you save the project brief.
When the AI makes something up and tells you about it with total confidence. It happens often with facts, prices, and web addresses.
The black window where you type commands to the computer instead of clicking. You don't need it here, only for Claude Code.
Claude installed on your computer with permission to create and edit your files itself. The next step once copy-paste wears you out.
